title: The Wardrobe of the coast road
premise: Mara Nakamura, a translator whose childhood language slips away word by word, returns to the coastal house of his late grandmother to settle her estate. Behind a wardrobe he finds a box of undelivered letters revealing she spent decades quietly protecting a neighbor from a wrongful conviction — and that his own father helped bury the truth. As the last bus route to the old neighborhood faces permanent rerouting, Mara must choose between loyalty to his family's silence and delivering the letters, saying goodbye out loud at last before the road itself disappears. He mails the final letter on the last bus's final run, and the truth, though it costs him his family name, finally arrives.
about_author: Coral Sterling is the pen name of a former court interpreter who grew up in a fading seaside town and writes about the words people refuse to say. This is their second novel.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Mara, POV first person, arrives at his grandmother's shuttered coastal house to catalog her belongings for sale. He notices his childhood language failing him mid-prayer at her grave. Emotional beat: grief tangled with guilt over years of unanswered letters he never sent.

chapters.title: What the Wardrobe Kept
chapters.summary: Moving the wardrobe to clear the room, Mara finds a false back panel and a box of forty undelivered letters addressed to Daniel Okafor, imprisoned thirty years ago. POV Mara. Beat: curiosity curdling into dread as he recognizes his father's handwriting on the earliest envelope.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter in third person: young Mara learning translation from his grandmother, who taught him that every borrowed word is a small betrayal. Present-day Mara begins reading the letters against her lessons. Beat: the theme of loyalty vs. truth takes root.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Vanished
chapters.summary: Mara tracks down Ruth Okafor, Daniel's sister, now running a dying bakery near the old bus depot. She remembers his family with cold courtesy. POV alternates Mara/Ruth. Beat: Mara realizes his father testified against Daniel — and lied.

chapters.title: Letters, Undelivered
chapters.summary: Reading deeper into the box, Mara discovers his grandmother wrote to Daniel monthly for decades, confessing what she witnessed the night of the crime, each letter sealed and never sent. POV Mara. Beat: horror that her courage stopped at the mailbox.

chapters.title: The Family Name
chapters.summary: Mara confronts his aging father, who admits the lie was 'necessary' to protect the family's business and reputation. Father threatens disinheritance. POV Mara. Beat: power's corruption made intimate; Mara wavers, tempted by the inheritance.

chapters.title: Rerouted
chapters.summary: Mara learns the council will permanently reroute the last bus from the old neighborhood in three weeks — severing Daniel's remaining ties to the world outside prison. POV Ruth. Beat: urgency ignites; justice outside the law must move on a timetable.

chapters.title: The Weight of Sealed Things
chapters.summary: Mara copies the letters, translating them into the language he is losing, finding fluency returning only when he speaks the truth aloud. His father discovers the copies and burns the originals' duplicates. Beat: rising tension peaks; betrayal begets betrayal.

chapters.title: Last Bus
chapters.summary: On the route's final night, Mara boards with the original letters, meets Ruth at the depot, and together they ride to the prison gates as the town watches. Climax: he hands the letters over publicly, renouncing his inheritance, speaking goodbye to his grandmother out loud in their dying tongue.

chapters.title: Delivered
chapters.summary: Weeks later, an inquiry reopens Daniel's case; his father's name is ruined, and Mara, estranged but unburdened, translates his grandmother's final unsent letter into English and reads it at her grave. Resolution: some words arrive late, but they still count as delivered.
